title: New Bounds for Kernel Sums via Fast Spherical Embeddings
claim: Prior methods each win only in separate regimes with a gap between them; ours covers the intermediate regime that neither handles best.
layout: 2 panels side by side, before left and after right, shaded regions
description: Two log-log plots share the same axes: x = 1/ε from 10^0 to 10^3, and y = Δ/σ from 10^0 to 10^6. In the left panel, a dashed diagonal line y=x splits the plane into two regions. The upper green region is labeled FJLT+RFF and the lower blue region is labeled Fastfood. In the right panel, the same two regions shrink to make room for a new peach-colored band labeled Ours. This band lies between an orange line y=x^2.5 and a blue line y=x^1/2, and the dashed y=x line still runs through its middle. FJLT+RFF stays in the green area above the orange line, and Fastfood stays in the blue area below the blue line. The eye goes first to the new peach band in the right panel.
caption: Best regime per method in Table 1, before (left) and after (right) ours, for Gaussian KDE in the high-dimensional case d ≳1/ε2 (in this regime, RFF is always subsumed by at least FJLT+RFF). The plots depict the trade-off between the inverse-error 1/ε on the x-axis and the effective diameter ∆σ = ∆/σ on the y-axis. The axes are in log scale.
abstract: We study query time bounds for the fundamental problem of estimating the kernel mean $\frac1{|X|}\sum_{x\in X}\mathbf{k}(x,y)$ of a query $y$ in a finite dataset $X\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ up to a prescribed additive error $\varepsilon$. The best known bounds for the Gaussian kernel are $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$, $\widetilde O(d+1/\varepsilon^4)$, and $\widetilde O(d+Î^2/\varepsilon^2)$, where $Î$ is the diameter of a region containing the points. We prove the new bound $\tilde O(d+\varepsilonÎ^2+1/\varepsilon^3)$, which improves over the previous ones in regimes with small error $\varepsilon$ and intermediate diameter $Î$. At the center of our proof is a new fast spherical embedding theorem in the sense introduced by Bartal, Recht and Schulman (2011), which limits the embedded data diameter while preserving local Euclidean distances and avoiding ``distance collapse'' at larger scales. This fast embedding theorem may be of independent interest.
